entry: Branch of physics concerned with solids, liquids and other condensed phases of matter. The field studies systems of many strongly interacting constituents, applying [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], electromagnetism and [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]] to predict the properties of very large groups of atoms. Subjects include [[Superconductivity|superconductivity]], [[Magnetism|magnetism]] and Bose–Einstein condensates. Crystallography, [[Metallurgy|metallurgy]] and elasticity were treated as separate areas until the 1940s, when they were grouped as [[Solid-state physics|solid-state physics]]; the study of liquids was added around the 1960s. As of 2009, one-third of American physicists identified as condensed matter physicists. According to physicist Manuel Cardona, [[Albert Einstein|Albert Einstein]] created the modern field with his 1905 article on the photoelectric effect and his 1907 article on the specific heat of solids.

Preparation added to food, typically after cooking, to enhance its flavor. Condiments include sauces added during cooking, such as [[Soy sauce|soy sauce]] and barbecue sauce; those added before serving, such as [[Mayonnaise|mayonnaise]] in a sandwich; and table condiments such as [[Ketchup|ketchup]], which diners add to taste. The word derives from the Latin *condimentum*, meaning "spice, seasoning, sauce," and originally described [[Pickling|pickled]] or preserved food. Condiments were known in [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]], India, Greece and China. The Romans made garum and liquamen by fermenting fish innards in salt, and the cookbook *Apicius* includes a section devoted to condiments. Global trade spread [[Spice|spices]] such as cinnamon, cumin and chile peppers into many cuisines. Condiments can also provide health benefits to diets that lack micronutrients.

Sheath-shaped barrier device worn during sexual intercourse to reduce the risk of pregnancy and [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infection]]. External, or male, condoms are usually made from latex, less commonly from [[Polyurethane|polyurethane]], polyisoprene or lamb intestine; internal, or female, condoms are typically made from polyurethane. With perfect use, women whose partners use external condoms have a 2% pregnancy rate per year; with typical use, the rate is 18% per year. Consistent latex use reduces the risk of [[HIV|HIV]] transmission by approximately 85%, according to a 2000 National Institutes of Health report, and greatly decreases the risk of [[Gonorrhea|gonorrhea]], [[Chlamydia|chlamydia]], trichomoniasis and hepatitis B. Condoms have been used to prevent infection since at least 1564; rubber condoms became available in 1855 and latex condoms in the 1920s. As of 2019, about 21% of people using [[Birth control|birth control]] used condoms, the second most common method after female sterilization (24%).

Family of highly venomous, predatory marine [[Gastropod|gastropods]] with cone-shaped shells. Cone snails use a barbed tooth, likened to a dart or harpoon and extended from the proboscis, to inject [[Venom|venom]] that paralyzes prey before they are engulfed. Venoms are mainly [[Peptide|peptide]]-based, and the sting of several larger species can be serious and even fatal to humans. Over 800 species were recognized as of March 2015, ranging from 1.3 cm to 21.6 cm long. Most live in warm tropical waters, with their greatest diversity in the Western Indo-Pacific.

Breakaway republic in the [[Southern United States|Southern United States]], 1861–1865, unrecognized as a sovereign nation by foreign governments or the United States. Seven states that had seceded from the Union formed the Confederacy on February 8, 1861, after the 1860 election of [[Abraham Lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]], with the principal aim of safeguarding [[Slavery|slavery]]. Its forces fought the [[American Civil War|Civil War]], and General [[Robert E. Lee|Robert E. Lee]] surrendered on April 9, 1865. Advocates of Lost Cause mythology, an idealized view of the Confederacy, later sought to sustain support for white supremacist policies such as the Jim Crow laws.

Formal alliance of [[Sovereign state|sovereign states]], usually created by a [[Treaty|treaty]], for common action. Confederations are typically formed to deal with issues such as defense, foreign relations, internal trade or currency, with the central government supporting all members. Member states retain their sovereignty and so generally have an implicit right of secession, although legal arrangements or centralization may constrain it. Compared with a federal state, the central authority is relatively weak: its decisions are agreements that member states must implement rather than laws acting directly on individuals, and decisions usually require consensus rather than a majority. These limits often create pressure to move toward a [[Federalism|federal system]], as in the American, Swiss and German cases. The Articles of Confederation, adopted by the thirteen American states in 1781, were replaced by the U.S. Constitution in 1789.

Range of values likely to contain an unknown statistical parameter, such as a population mean. In frequentist inference, a confidence interval has lower and upper bounds derived from a [[Sampling (statistics)|random sample]], at a pre-defined confidence level typically 95%. The level describes long-run performance: if the same sampling procedure were repeated 100 times, approximately 95 of the intervals would contain the true population mean. It does not mean that one interval has a 95% probability of containing the parameter; that interpretation applies to credible intervals in [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian inference]].

Matching of attitudes, beliefs and behaviors to [[Social norm|group norms]]. Conformity may result from subtle unconscious influences or direct social pressure, and it can occur when a person is alone, as when following social norms while eating or watching television. In Solomon Asch's line-judgment experiments, about one-third (32%) of participants sided with a clearly incorrect majority on critical trials, and about 75% conformed at least once across 12 critical trials. [[Psychology|Psychologists]] distinguish normative influence, driven by fear of rejection, from informational influence, which arises when people believe a group is better informed. According to Herbert Kelman, conformity takes three forms: compliance, identification and internalization. [[Culture|Culture]], gender, age and group size all affect its degree, and minority influence can sometimes shift the majority. Conformity can also be beneficial, as in driving on the conventionally approved side of the road.

Multi-industry company that owns subsidiaries operating in several unrelated industries. Conglomerates can form through mergers, acquisitions, spin-offs or joint ventures, and they seek economies of scale and risk diversification, though they face complexity, bureaucracy and agency problems. In the [[United States|United States]], a "conglomerate fad" of the 1960s proved to be an economic bubble, and many conglomerates collapsed or were broken up in the 1980s due to poor performance, accounting scandals and antitrust regulation. They have remained prevalent in Asia, including [[South Korea|South Korea]], where they often have strong government ties.

[[Sedimentary rock|Sedimentary rock]] made of rounded gravel-sized pieces, called clasts, set in a finer matrix. The matrix, which may be [[Sand|sand]], silt or [[Clay|clay]], is typically cemented by [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]], iron oxide, silica or hardened clay. Conglomerates form when rounded gravels deposited by water or [[Glacier|glaciers]] solidify and cement over time. They are closely related to sandstones in origin and probably make up less than 1% of all sedimentary rocks by weight. [[Breccia|Breccias]] are similar but have angular clasts. Conglomerates contain at least 30% rounded to subangular clasts larger than 2 mm in diameter. Orthoconglomerates, whose clasts touch each other, are typically cross-bedded and associated with flowing water, while paraconglomerates float in matrix and are often glacial tills or debris flow deposits.

Absolute monarchy in [[Central Africa|Central Africa]], 1885–1908, privately owned by [[Leopold II of Belgium|King Leopold II]]. Leopold claimed the Congo Basin through the International Association of the Congo, persuading European states at the Berlin Conference that he was involved in humanitarian work. The state covered most of the present [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. It extracted ivory, rubber and minerals through concessionary companies. Forced labor, torture and killings were reported. The Casement Report of 1903 led to the arrest and punishment of officials responsible for killings during a rubber-collecting expedition. The atrocities inspired [[Joseph Conrad|Joseph Conrad]]'s novel *Heart of Darkness*. Estimates of deaths vary: the highest state that 50% of the population in the rubber provinces died, but the lack of accurate records makes the toll difficult to quantify. In 1908 the Belgian Parliament annexed the state as the Belgian Congo, after public pressure.

Second-longest river in Africa, after the [[Nile|Nile]], flowing through Central Africa. Formerly known as the Zaire River, it is the third-largest river in the world by discharge volume, after the Amazon and Ganges–Brahmaputra. It is the world's deepest recorded river, with depths of around 220 m (720 ft). The Congo–Lualaba–Luvua–Luapula–Chambeshi river system has an overall length of 4,700 km, and the river is the only major river to cross the [[Equator|equator]] twice. Its drainage basin covers 4,014,500 sq km, the second largest of any river after the Amazon, and the river discharges an average of 41,000 m³/s at its mouth. The name Congo derives from the [[Kingdom of Kongo|Kingdom of Kongo]] on the river's southern bank. The [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Democratic Republic of the Congo]] and the [[Republic of the Congo|Republic of the Congo]] are both named after it.

Belt of lowland tropical moist broadleaf forest across the [[Congo River|Congo River]] basin in Central Africa. Covering over 2,000,000 sq km across six countries, the Congolian rainforests are the world's second-largest tropical forest, after the [[Amazon rainforest|Amazon rainforest]]. They contain a quarter of the world's remaining tropical forest and more than 10,000 plant species, of which 30% are endemic. The region is home to over 10,000 animal species, including the western lowland gorilla, one of the world's most threatened primates, and the [[Okapi|okapi]], which is endemic to the northeastern forests. The central Congo Basin's peat swamp forests store about 29 billion tons of carbon. Annual forest loss of 0.3% during the 2000s gave the region the lowest deforestation rate of any major tropical forest zone.

Diplomatic conference of the major European powers, held in Berlin from June 13 to July 13, 1878. It revised the terms that the Russian Empire had imposed on the Ottoman Empire under the Treaty of San Stefano, which had ended the [[Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)|Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878]]. British opposition to a Russian-aligned Greater Bulgaria drove the talks, and [[Otto von Bismarck|Otto von Bismarck]], chancellor of the German Empire, acted as mediator. The resulting Treaty of Berlin, signed July 13, 1878, essentially dismantled the Greater Bulgarian state. [[Austria-Hungary|Austria-Hungary]] occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina, Britain took possession of Cyprus, and Romania, Serbia and Montenegro were recognized as independent. The [[Ottoman Empire|Ottomans]] were humiliated, Russia resented the lack of rewards, and Serbia, Bulgaria and Greece received far less than they thought they deserved. The settlement deepened Balkan tensions that foreshadowed the [[Balkan Wars|Balkan Wars]] and the [[World War I|First World War]].

Series of diplomatic meetings held in [[Vienna|Vienna]] from September 1814 to June 1815 to settle Europe after the downfall of [[Napoleon|Napoleon]]. Chaired by Austrian statesman [[Klemens von Metternich|Klemens von Metternich]], the Congress aimed to balance the major powers so they could remain at peace, while restraining republican, liberal and revolutionary movements. France gave up Napoleon's conquests, while Prussia, Austria and Russia made major territorial gains. The Congress ratified the new [[Kingdom of the Netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]], meant to serve as a buffer between the [[German Confederation|German Confederation]] and France. The agreement was signed nine days before Napoleon's final defeat at Waterloo on June 18, 1815, and negotiations continued despite the renewed fighting of the [[Hundred Days|Hundred Days]]. Historians disagree about its legacy. Critics argue that it suppressed national, democratic and liberal movements, while others credit it with protecting Europe from large wars for almost a century.

Curve formed when a plane intersects the surface of a cone. The three types are the [[Ellipse|ellipse]], [[Parabola|parabola]] and [[Hyperbola|hyperbola]]; a [[Circle|circle]] is a special case of the ellipse. Ancient Greek mathematicians studied conic sections, culminating around 200 BC in the systematic work of [[Apollonius of Perga|Apollonius of Perga]]. A conic can also be defined by a focus, a directrix and a fixed ratio called the eccentricity: an ellipse has eccentricity between 0 and 1, a parabola has eccentricity 1, and a hyperbola has eccentricity greater than 1. A circle's eccentricity is defined to be zero. In [[Analytic geometry|analytic geometry]], a conic is a plane algebraic curve of degree 2, given by an equation of the form Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0. Conic sections also describe planetary [[Orbit|orbits]] and satellite trajectories.

Group of woody, mostly evergreen [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperm]] plants that bear cones. There are over 600 living species. Each tree produces separate male and female cones, and the seeds are usually dispersed by wind. Conifers first appeared more than 300 million years ago in the [[Carboniferous|Carboniferous]] and dominated land plants during the Mesozoic, until [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] took over many ecosystems in the [[Cretaceous|Cretaceous]]. Conifers dominate the [[Taiga|taiga]] of the Northern Hemisphere, where conical shapes shed snow and waxy needle-shaped leaves limit water loss. The tallest living tree is a coast redwood, 116.07 m tall, and the oldest non-clonal living tree is a Great Basin bristlecone pine, 4,700 years old. As of 2025, 94 conifer species were listed as endangered. Conifers are of great economic value for timber and paper production.

Highly poisonous flowering plant in the [[Apiaceae|carrot family]]. *Conium maculatum*, commonly called hemlock or poison hemlock, is a biennial [[Weed|weed]] native to [[Europe|Europe]] and North Africa. It has spread to Australia, West Asia and North and South America, where it can become invasive. All parts are toxic, especially the seeds and roots. It is best known as the poison that killed the philosopher [[Socrates|Socrates]] after his trial in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]].

Mathematical proposition put forward on a tentative basis, without proof. A conjecture is considered proven only when it is shown to be logically impossible to be false, and it becomes a [[Theorem|theorem]] once proved. Finding no counterexample is not proof: the [[Collatz conjecture|Collatz conjecture]] has been tested for all integers up to 1.2 trillion, yet a very large counterexample could still exist. Many important theorems were once conjectures. The [[Poincaré conjecture|Poincaré conjecture]] was resolved through the Geometrization theorem, and [[Fermat's Last Theorem|Fermat's Last Theorem]] was proven by Andrew Wiles. Some conjectures are independent of accepted [[Axiom|axioms]]: the continuum hypothesis was shown to be independent of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory, so it can be adopted or rejected as a new axiom.

[[Twin|Twins]] whose bodies are joined in the womb. Conjoined twins occur in an estimated one in 50,000 to one in 200,000 births. Approximately half are stillborn, and an additional one-third die within 24 hours. The generally accepted cause is [[Fission (biology)|fission]], in which a fertilized egg splits partially. Chang and Eng Bunker, born in Siam, were joined at the torso by a band of flesh and cartilage and by their fused livers. They became known as the Siamese Twins, and the term came to be associated with conjoined twins generally.

Part of speech that connects words, [[Phrase|phrases]] or [[Clause|clauses]], called its conjuncts. A conjunction is an invariant, non-inflecting particle that stands between its conjuncts. Whether a word is a conjunction depends on each language's [[Grammar|grammar]]; in English, *after* can be a preposition or a conjunction, depending on syntax. Idiomatic phrases such as "as well as" can also function as conjunctions. Coordinating conjunctions, such as and, but, or, nor, for, so and yet, join structures of equal rank, while subordinating conjunctions, such as because, although and if, introduce dependent clauses. Commas often separate clauses, and some style guides require a comma before a coordinating conjunction that joins two independent clauses.

[[Inflammation|Inflammation]] of the conjunctiva, the thin, clear layer covering the white of the eye and the inner eyelid, also called pink eye. Symptoms include redness, pain, itchiness, increased tears and eyelids stuck shut in the morning. Most infections in adults are viral, often accompanying a [[Common cold|common cold]], while bacterial causes predominate in children. Allergies to pollen or animal hair are also common. Viral cases usually have no specific treatment, and antibiotics can shorten bacterial illness. Between three and six million people in the United States get acute conjunctivitis each year.

[[U.S. state|U.S. state]] in the [[New England|New England]] region of the [[Northeastern United States|Northeastern United States]]. It is the third-smallest state by area, with more than 3.6 million residents as of 2024. Its capital is Hartford. The state is named after the Connecticut River. Its nickname, the Constitution State, refers to the Fundamental Orders of 1639, considered by some to be the first written constitution in Western history. Connecticut was one of the [[Thirteen Colonies|Thirteen Colonies]] that rejected British rule during the [[American Revolution|American Revolution]], and in January 1788 it became the fifth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.

Biological tissue found between other tissues in the body, one of four primary types of animal tissue. Most connective tissue consists of elastic and collagen fibers, ground substance and cells, including fibroblasts, adipocytes, macrophages, mast cells and leukocytes. It develops mostly from mesenchyme, which derives from the mesoderm. The three meninges that envelop the brain and spinal cord are connective tissue, and [[Blood|blood]] and lymph are classed as specialized fluid connective tissues. Connective tissue proper includes loose and dense varieties, while special connective tissue includes supportive [[Bone|bone]] and [[Cartilage|cartilage]]. [[Tendon|Tendons]] and [[Ligament|ligaments]] are examples of dense regular connective tissue, in which collagen fibers run parallel for strength in one direction. Type I collagen makes up about 25% of the total protein content of the mammalian body. The term was introduced in 1830 by Johannes Peter Müller.

Irish professional [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial artist]] and former two-division champion in the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship|Ultimate Fighting Championship]]. He was the first fighter to hold UFC titles in two weight classes simultaneously. He lost a boxing bout to [[Floyd Mayweather Jr.|Floyd Mayweather Jr.]] by tenth-round technical knockout. In November 2024, an Irish High Court ruled in a civil case that he had assaulted and raped a woman, ordering him to pay over €248,000 in damages. He lost an appeal on the verdict in July 2025.
